title: Severe Pre-Eclampsia and Eclampsia: Emergency Management

pathophysiology.summary: Pre-eclampsia occurs after 20 weeks' gestation with hypertension and proteinuria; severe features include severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, raised liver enzymes (ALT above 70 IU/L) and platelets below 100 ×10⁹/L. Severe hypertension (160/110 mmHg or higher) needs admission and immediate treatment in critical care. Eclampsia is a seizure in pre-eclampsia; magnesium sulfate is given, and diazepam or phenytoin are not used instead. Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome is a severe variant. Excess fluid is harmful, so maintenance fluids are restricted.

symptoms: Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, vomiting.
redFlags: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) above 70 IU/L, platelets below 150 ×10⁹/L (below 100 ×10⁹/L is severe) or creatinine 90 µmol/L or higher.
Blood pressure uncontrolled despite three classes of antihypertensive.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and platelets below 100 ×10⁹/L; do not give dexamethasone or betamethasone to treat HELLP syndrome.
Slow to wake or focal signs: check pupils and obtain computed tomography (CT) of the head.
Blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg and normal bloods; manage as hypertension.

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate treatment
actions: Admit; measure blood pressure every 15 to 30 minutes until below 160/110 mmHg.
Treat severe hypertension immediately in critical care with labetalol (oral or IV), oral nifedipine or IV hydralazine; target 135/85 mmHg or less in NG133.
Give IV magnesium sulfate for severe hypertension or severe pre-eclampsia with a current or previous eclamptic fit; consider it if birth is planned within 24 hours or severe features appear.
Do not use diazepam, phenytoin or other anticonvulsants instead of magnesium sulfate.

clinicalManagement.title: Magnesium sulfate regimen
actions: NG133: 4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes, then 1 g per hour for 24 hours; after a fit continue 24 hours after the last fit; recurrent fit: further 2 g to 4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes.
Check reflexes and respiratory rate regularly and monitor urine output.
Consider neonatal calcium and magnesium monitoring if use is prolonged or repeated beyond 5 to 7 days.

clinicalManagement.title: Fluids and monitoring
actions: Limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL per hour unless other fluid losses; avoid volume expansion unless hydralazine is the antihypertensive, when up to 500 mL crystalloid may be considered with the first dose.
Blood tests (platelets, ALT, creatinine) twice weekly with mild-to-moderate hypertension and three times weekly with severe hypertension.
CTG at diagnosis; fetal growth, amniotic fluid and Doppler at diagnosis and every 2 weeks when managing conservatively.
If early birth within 7 days is likely, offer antenatal corticosteroids; do not use them to treat HELLP syndrome.

clinicalManagement.title: Timing of birth
actions: Planned early birth if blood pressure cannot be controlled with 3 or more classes of antihypertensive, or oxygen saturation falls below 90%.
At 37 weeks or later, initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours.
In labour, measure blood pressure hourly, or every 15 to 30 minutes until below 160/110 mmHg in severe hypertension; do not preload with IV fluids before epidural.

clinicalManagement.title: Postnatal care
actions: Blood pressure at least four times daily as an inpatient; start treatment if 150/100 mmHg or higher.
Check platelets, transaminases and creatinine at 48 to 72 hours; repeat until normal if abnormal.
Transfer to community care when symptom-free, blood pressure 150/100 mmHg or lower with or without treatment, and blood results stable or improving.
